results.term_definition:
In our Solar System, the outer planets are Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. Their orbits are outside the asteroid belt, and all of those planets are so-called giant planets, with an extremely thick atmosphere made up mostly of hydrogen. This makes them physically distinct from the inner planets, each of which is a comparatively small rocky body with a comparatively thin atmosphere. 

Planets around stars other than our Sun do not necessarily fall into inner and outer groups with similar characteristics – we know a number of stars with at least one gas giant, a "hot Jupiter", in close orbit.
